sections.text_helper: Section 30.3.7 "Private keys protection using CCB" in chapter 30 (Public key accelerator (PKA)), RM0522 Rev 1, page 923.
sections.section_content:
Chaining modes
As shown in Figure217, setting CCOP to a value different from 0 in the CCB peripheral
automatically activates a chaining mechanism between PKA, RNG, and SAES, depending
on the OPSTEP value (see Table241), then sets the CCEN bit in the PKA_SR register.
For the effect of different OPSTEP values in each protected operation (ECDSA signature,
scalar multiplication, modular exponentiation), refer to Section30.3.7: Private keys
protection using CCB.
[Figure 217. Chaining of PKA with SAES or RNG]
CCB
RNG
CCOP 0
SAES
PKA
CCEN = 1
[Table 241. Chaining mode to/from PKA]
When the application uses a PKA protected operation (with its private key), it must load the
related blob information in the PKA RAM and in the SAES_DINR register. If the information
exactly matches the conditions of the blob generation (the choice and order of writing
protected parameters in PKA RAM, the selection of blob encryption key, and the usage of
the original encrypted secrets), the CCB allows it to set the START bit in PKA_CR. When
the PKA ignores the setting of the START bit, the application must reset the CCB using the
IPRST bit in CCB_CR, then start the protected operation sequence again.
A protected application typically uses the PKA in the following sequence composed of three
phases.
Step 1: Public phase
Before using a protected operation, the application may need to write unprotected
parameters to the PKA RAM, as defined in Table241.
Step 2: Integrity protected phase
To use a PKA operation, the application must load specific parameters in PKA RAM. When
CCEN bit is set in PKA_SR, the integrity protected parameters defined in Table242 must
always be written in the same way. Integrity protection is enforced in specific OPSTEPs, as
defined in Table241.
Typical issues with integrity of protected operation parameters are:
• The blob encryption key loaded in SAES registers is not correct.
• At least one confidentiality protected parameter defined in Table243 has an incorrect
value, or was not properly written (DATAOKF=0 or RNGOKF=0, see PKA status
register (PKA_SR)).
• At least one integrity protected parameter defined in Table242 has an incorrect value,
is written at an incorrect address, or its write sequence to PKA RAM does not match
the sequence used during the blob creation. On this specific point, the application must
follow the sequence detailed in Table242 when writing each item described in the
column Parameters.
CCB feeds integrity protected parameters to SAES during the header phase of AES-GCM
(GCMPH=0x1).
[Table 242. Integrity protected parameters list]
Step 3: Confidentiality phase
To use any PKA protected operation, the application must load confidentiality protected
parameters in the PKA RAM. When the CCEN bit is set in PKA_SR, the parameters defined
in Table243 are protected in confidentiality by:
• Making PKA RAM write-only
• Triggering a MODE[5:0] error (MDERRF) in PKA_SR when MODE[5:0] bitfiled in
PKA_CR does not match the expected value when application sets START bit in
PKA_CR
• Monitoring the correct management of protected parameters through DATAOKF and
RNGOKF flags (see PKA status register (PKA_SR))
• Optionally, generating ECC secrets from the on-chip TRNG when CCOP=0xC2 or
0x82 and OPSTEP=0x6, and when CCOP=0xC3 and OPSTEP=0x16. The PKA
performs a sanity check before accepting this random value (see the RNGERRF flag).
Confidentiality protected parameters are described in Table243. CCB feeds them to SAES
during the payload phase of the AES-GCM (GCMPH = 0x2).
[Table 243. Confidentiality protected parameter list]
Step 4: Running PKA protected operation
Set the START bit in PKA_CR. When the whole sequence executes correctly, the PKA RAM
becomes inaccessible for reading and writing. Input parameters are automatically erased
when the PROCENDF flag in PKA_SR is set, or if the application aborts the current
operation by clearing the EN bit in PKA_CR.
